extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of political theory and American history
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply criteria Tocqueville uses to judge the future condition and durability of a federal union (here, the United States). The criteria cover material interests, shared opinions, demographic change, institutional tendencies, and cultural differences that affect cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of economic interests across regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Union is strengthened when different regions' economic productions are complementary and interdependent (e.g., South supplies raw materials, North supplies manufactures and shipping), so that union promotes interchange and increases value by facilitating consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville argues that distinct regional economies are not necessarily hostile; rather, when complementary they create mutual material incentives to preserve the confederation (examples: North shipping Southern/Western produce; South/West relying on Northern commercial resources and navy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of hostile contrary interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The durability of a vast union depends on lack of directly opposing interests among provinces; the mere existence of different interests does not threaten union unless they are hostile to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between mere difference and genuine hostility — a large territory is prejudicial only when provinces' interests terminate in open dissensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared opinions and public sentiment (moral/political unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Society endures not merely because people obey the same laws, but because many hold the same opinions and feel similarly; public opinion and common principles bind the nation more than formal authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville emphasizes shared beliefs in popular sovereignty, liberty, equality, freedom of the press, right of association, jury, and official responsibility as foundations of social unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common immaterial interests (political & moral principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity in political, religious, moral and philosophical principles (e.g., belief in people as source of power, faith in perfectibility, value of knowledge) fosters cohesion across wide territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These shared convictions act as an instinctive agreement that sustains society even across multiple sovereign units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual dependence on federal protection and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of the union support the central government because it secures common material goods (e.g., navy protection, commercial routes) that individual states could not secure alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Southern/Western reliance on Northern shipping and a federal navy to protect exports; federal budget contributions therefore support shared material interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of slavery on character and manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery does not necessarily create opposing material interests between regions, but it alters manners and character in ways that can undermine social cohesion (e.g., Southern citizens accustomed to command and idleness vs. Northern citizens accustomed to self-reliance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville links slavery to the development of superciliousness, impatience, indolence in the South and contrasts it with Northern habits of industry, patience, and practical knowledge — cultural divergence that can threaten unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population size and territorial extent as a hazard
rubrics_metrics.description: Very large population and extensive territory with many distinct peoples/states of unequal strength increase the difficulty of maintaining a lasting federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville reasons that forty distinct peoples over half of Europe make avoiding rivalry and ambition unlikely; sheer scale plus unequal strength threaten continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproportionate growth among states (preponderance risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid and uneven increase in population or wealth of some states produces fears of domination in others and may provoke mistrust, envy, and threats of secession from those that feel diminished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He cites New York's growth and the declining federal influence felt by Southern states as a cause of southern uneasiness and political agitation (example: tariff controversy and South Carolina nullification rhetoric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual weakness and small number of parties favor union
rubrics_metrics.description: Union is easier to sustain when contracting parties are individually weak and limited in number because their safety depends on the collective compact; stronger, larger members feel less necessity for the federal tie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville notes smaller states in 1790 felt insignificance and were more compliant; as states grow (e.g., New York), they may accept union for prosperity but seek preponderance, reducing unanimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instability due to frontier settlement and settler character
rubrics_metrics.description: Frontier settlers, often adventurers lacking traditions and social restraints, are more impatient of governance and less constrained by law and morality, which can weaken national cohesion when they rapidly acquire political influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The West's settlers may reach government before learning self-government; the empire of law and morality is weaker among them, creating temporary dangers to the Union's stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifting demographic center and political gravitation
rubrics_metrics.description: As population shifts (e.g., inland towards Mississippi valley), the center of federal power and influence shifts too; this change can produce political preponderance of new regions and resentment in older parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville notes census-based representation changes and predicts Mississippi basin will become the future center, altering federal policy direction and provoking old states' loss of leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural geography and infrastructure affecting regional power
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical geography (harbors, rivers, coast quality) and maritime infrastructure shape commercial advantage, population growth, and thus political influence of regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Northern ports with deep harbors foster shipping and manufacturing growth; Southern coasts with obstructed river mouths limit commercial advantages, contributing to North's superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pace of social change (rapidity increases danger)
rubrics_metrics.description: Very rapid societal transformation (population doubling, rapid founding of towns/states) exacerbates instability because generations cannot adjust and resentments accumulate quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville contrasts slow generational change with the American 'precipitate' progress where a citizen may see his state's preponderance rise or fall within his lifetime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two modes of union dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union can perish either by an explicit secession of a confederate state or by gradual erosion of federal authority through tacit consent, leaving the central power impotent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He distinguishes sudden withdrawal (secession) from progressive internal enervation (senile inaptitude) that paralyzes government and eventually leads to breakdown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of federal existence on continued assent
rubrics_metrics.description: The confederation's survival depends on the ongoing consent and assent of its member states; the federal compact is voluntary and must be continually reaffirmed by the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a foundational normative principle: without continued assent, the federal bond can unravel either overtly or imperceptibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear of centralization and popular suspicion of encroaching power
rubrics_metrics.description: Widespread American antipathy to centralization acts as a check on federal growth but also encourages politicians to court majorities by attacking central power; this political culture shapes institutional evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville warns that such popular distrust can obscure the different dynamics in a union of distinct communities versus a single people and can produce institutional paralysis or fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural divergence from slavery and equality of fortunes
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in social structure (e.g., equality of fortunes and absence of servitude in North) produce distinct habits: industrious, practical, and self-reliant northern character versus southern aristocratic tastes — cultural divergence that affects political concord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville links social-economic formation to temperament: northern citizens focus on pecuniary advantage and practical application of knowledge; southern citizens prize grandeur, leisure, and renown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political consequences of economic policy perceived as regional favoritism
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law or policy is perceived as benefiting one region at another's expense (e.g., tariffs seen as enriching North and ruining South), it provokes protest and may catalyze secessionist sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case: South Carolina's nullification claim that tariffs enriched North while harming Southern economy; perception of abuse of federal power stokes threats to union.
